issues.legal_issue: A deeming rule for a landlord’s residential requirement applies only when the tenant’s accommodation and the landlord-occupied remainder form parts of one unit of accommodation, not merely because they are in the same structure.
material_facts: The ground floor had two separate tenements: the tenant occupied one and the landlord occupied the other for residential purposes.
The lower authorities treated the ground floor as a building to which the deeming rule applied, without deciding whether the two tenements together formed a single unit of accommodation.
issues.conclusion: The deeming rule applies only when the accommodation under tenancy and the accommodation occupied by the landlord together constitute one unit; separate and independent units do not qualify. The matter was remanded for the lower court to apply that construction.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 21(1)(a) and Explanation (iv) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, the phrase referring to a building of which the tenanted building is a part requires a single unit of accommodation. Because the Explanation creates a conclusive presumption favouring the landlord in tenant-protective legislation, it must be construed strictly against the landlord. The Court approved the construction in Chunnoo Lal v. Additional District Judge, Allahabad.

predicates.residential_release_proceeding: A landlord seeks release of rented accommodation for residential use.
predicates.tenant_occupies_part_of_single_unit: The tenant occupies part of one unit of accommodation, rather than an independent unit in a larger structure.
predicates.landlord_resides_in_remainder: The landlord occupies the remaining part of that same unit for residential purposes.

issues.definition: When a residential release proceeding concerns one unit divided between the tenant and a residentially occupying landlord, the landlord’s requirement is conclusively established.

issues.legal_issue: Comparative hardship need not be assessed when the statutory deeming rule for bona fide requirement applies.
material_facts: The landlord relied on the deeming rule because the tenant occupied part of the ground floor while the landlord occupied the remainder for residential purposes.
The District Court found that the tenant would suffer greater hardship if release were granted, but the High Court held that hardship was immaterial if the deeming rule applied.
issues.conclusion: If the deeming rule applies, the relative hardship of landlord and tenant is not considered, and the landlord is entitled to release once the rule’s conditions are satisfied.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 21(1) requires consideration of likely hardship except in cases covered by the Explanation. Where Explanation (iv) applies, the proviso has no application and comparative hardship is irrelevant.

predicates.residential_release_proceeding: A landlord seeks release of rented accommodation for residential use.
predicates.deeming_rule_conditions_satisfied: The tenant’s accommodation and the landlord’s residentially occupied remainder satisfy the conditions for the statutory deeming rule.

issues.definition: In a residential release proceeding, if the conditions for the deeming rule are satisfied, comparative hardship need not be assessed.

issues.legal_issue: Whether the deeming rule applies to the facts is a mixed question of law and fact that may be corrected in writ review when the lower court applied an erroneous interpretation.
material_facts: The lower authorities held that the deeming rule applied to the ground-floor accommodation.
The High Court treated that determination as an unreviewable finding of fact, although its application depended on the correct interpretation of the rule.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could correct the lower court’s conclusion because applicability of the deeming rule is a mixed question of law and fact, and the High Court’s contrary view was erroneous.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, a High Court may correct a conclusion resting on an erroneous interpretation where applying the law to the facts presents a mixed question of law and fact; the conclusion is not insulated from review merely because lower courts described it as a finding of fact.

predicates.writ_review_proceeding: A party challenges a lower court’s decision in writ review.
predicates.legal_interpretation_determines_applicat: Whether a legal rule applies depends on applying its correct interpretation to the case facts.
predicates.lower_court_used_erroneous_interpretatio: The lower court reached its conclusion by applying an incorrect interpretation of the legal rule.

issues.definition: In writ review, when a legal rule’s application depends on the facts and the lower court used an erroneous interpretation, the High Court may correct the resulting conclusion.

issues.legal_issue: When the deeming rule is unavailable or inapplicable and the tenant would suffer greater hardship, the landlord’s release application fails.
material_facts: The District Court found that the tenant would suffer greater hardship from release than the landlord would suffer from refusal.

The Supreme Court left the effect of the later omission of the deeming rule for the District Court to determine and directed that, if the landlord could not rely on the rule or it did not apply, the release application would fail.
issues.conclusion: If the landlord cannot rely on the deeming rule or its conditions are not met, the application fails on the existing finding that the tenant would suffer greater hardship.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 21(1) requires comparative hardship to be considered where the case is not covered by the Explanation. The District Court’s finding that the tenant would suffer greater hardship was not disturbed; the Court expressly stated that the application would fail if the deeming rule could not be relied on or did not apply.

predicates.residential_release_proceeding: A landlord seeks release of rented accommodation.
predicates.deeming_rule_unavailable_or_inapplicable: The landlord cannot rely on the deeming rule, or the facts do not satisfy its conditions.
predicates.tenant_would_suffer_greater_hardship: The tenant would suffer greater hardship from release than the landlord would suffer from refusal.

issues.definition: A residential release application fails when the deeming rule is unavailable or inapplicable and release would cause the tenant greater hardship.
